front.title: Cryptographic Proof of Effort (CPoE): Architecture and Evidence Format

abstract.t: This document specifies the Cryptographic Proof of Effort (CPoE) Evidence Framework, a specialized profile of Remote Attestation Procedures (RATS) designed to validate the provenance of effort in digital authorship. Unlike traditional provenance, which tracks file custody, CPoE proves sustained computational effort and behavioral patterns consistent with human authorship by entangling content hashes with temporal, behavioral, and physical constraints. Technical specifications for wire formats, sequential work functions, and hardware-anchored trust are provided.

note.name: Discussion Venues
note.t: Source for this draft and an issue tracker can be found at https://github.com/writerslogic/draft-condrey-cpoe.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence has created an authenticity crisis in digital discourse. While traditional provenance tracks the "custody of pixels," it fails to attest that genuine human effort was expended in creation. This document specifies the Cryptographic Proof of Effort (CPoE) protocol, which extends the RATS architecture to validate the "provenance of effort."

Unlike traditional attestation which captures static system state, CPoE proves that sustained cognitive and computational effort was expended during authorship. Its Sequential Work Function (SWF) enforces temporal monotonicity, jitter seals bind behavioral entropy (human inter-keystroke timing) to the checkpoint chain, and entangled MACs bind physical state (thermodynamics) to the document's evolution.

By entangling content hashes with these physical constraints, this protocol enables an Attester to generate an Evidence Packet (.cpoe) that imposes quantifiable cost on forgery of authorship claims, preserving privacy by design without disclosing document content. The formal threat model, including the adversarial Attester assumption that distinguishes CPoE from standard RATS deployments, is defined in .

This document is a companion to , which specifies the Verifier's forensic appraisal logic, the Attestation Result (WAR) wire format, and the quantitative security model. Implementers of Verifier components require both documents.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Problem Statement
section.t: Digital documents lack provenance of effort. Existing cryptographic mechanisms address complementary aspects -- COSE signatures prove key possession, trusted timestamps prove temporal existence, and media provenance standards track post-creation custody -- but none reveals how a document was produced or evolved during authorship.
Non-cryptographic approaches have emerged to address this gap, but each carries fundamental limitations:

dd.t: Screen recording, keystroke logging, and similar monitoring capture authoring activity but are inherently privacy-invasive, require continuous trust in a third-party archive, and produce evidence that cannot be independently verified without access to the surveillance infrastructure.

Stylometric classifiers and AI-generated content detectors operate on finished output rather than the effort of creation. These tools are probabilistic, degrade as generative models improve, are vulnerable to adversarial evasion, and exhibit systematic bias against non-native language speakers . Their outputs do not constitute deterministic, independently reproducible evidence.

Several products have emerged to fill this gap but lack openness, verifiability, or both. GPTZero ships a Chrome extension that records writing replay in Google Docs and analyzes typing patterns using a proprietary algorithm ; the analysis is opaque, controlled by the detector rather than the author, and not independently reproducible. The Authors Guild "Human Authored" certification for books relies on author self-attestation with no cryptographic verification . Amazon requires publishers to disclose AI-generated content on its Kindle Direct Publishing platform but provides no mechanism to verify compliance .

section.t: The need for effort-based provenance extends across sectors and jurisdictions. AI-assisted authoring is entering clinical documentation workflows, prompting the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services to seek input on how to maintain accountability when AI tools contribute to medical records . The autonomous content generation capabilities of AI agents have led the National Institute of Standards and Technology to examine security implications, including the attribution of agent-produced output . The common requirement across these sectors is a standardized, open mechanism to verify how content was produced rather than inferring it after the fact. Such a mechanism must satisfy four properties:

li.t: Privacy-preserving: Evidence must not require disclosure of document content or invasive behavioral surveillance. Cryptographic hashes, not raw content, must form the evidentiary basis.
Independently verifiable: Proofs must be self-contained and deterministically checkable by any Verifier without access to external archives or proprietary systems.
Tamper-evident: Evidence must form a cryptographic chain resistant to retroactive modification, reordering, or selective omission.
Effort-documenting: The mechanism must capture the effort expended as a document evolved over time, not merely what it contains at a point in time.

section.name: Use Cases
section.t: The provenance gap identified in has concrete consequences across multiple domains. Where detection-based methods have been deployed as substitutes for effort-based proof, the results have been problematic: Liang et al. found that GPT detectors misclassified over 61% of essays by non-native English writers as AI-generated , and courts have begun ruling that sanctions based solely on AI detection scores lack valid evidentiary basis. The following use cases illustrate how effort-based proof addresses needs that neither content detection nor custody-based provenance can satisfy.

Importantly, CPoE does not assert that human-authored content is inherently superior to AI-generated content. The value of proving effort lies in transparency: enabling Relying Parties to make informed trust decisions appropriate to their context. In some contexts, AI-generated content is entirely acceptable or even preferred; in others, stakeholders require assurance about the nature and extent of human involvement. CPoE provides the evidentiary basis for these decisions without imposing a policy preference.

section.name: Creative Industries and Labor Rights
section.t: Professional guilds and labor organizations in the creative industries have established contractual frameworks governing AI use in content production. The Writers Guild of America's 2023 Minimum Basic Agreement provides that AI-generated material cannot be credited as "literary material" and requires studios to disclose when materials provided to writers incorporate AI-generated content. Similar provisions exist in SAG-AFTRA agreements for digital replicas and synthetic performers, and the Authors Guild has published model contract clauses addressing AI use.

These contractual obligations currently lack a standardized technical enforcement mechanism. A screenwriter's authoring application acts as the Attester, producing an Evidence Packet (.cpoe) that documents the effort of writing. When the writer uses AI tools for research or drafting, the Tool Receipt Protocol defined in records each AI contribution with a signed receipt binding the tool's output to the evidence chain. The studio or guild acts as the Relying Party, consuming the Attestation Result (.cwar) to verify compliance with contractual AI disclosure requirements. The Attestation Result includes the human-to-machine effort ratio, providing quantified attribution rather than a binary human-or-AI determination.

section.name: Academic Integrity
section.t: Educational institutions face a dilemma: post-hoc AI detectors produce probabilistic scores that cannot reliably distinguish AI-generated text from the writing of non-native speakers, students with certain disabilities, or those with concise writing styles . Sanctions based on detector output alone have been overturned by courts as lacking valid evidentiary basis, with affected families incurring substantial legal costs. Institutions that rely on these tools expose themselves to litigation under due process and civil rights frameworks.

CPoE inverts this model. Rather than accusing students based on statistical analysis of their output, it enables students to voluntarily submit affirmative evidence of their authorship effort. The student's writing environment acts as the Attester, producing an Evidence Packet over the course of the assignment. The institution's learning management system acts as the Relying Party, evaluating whether the submitted evidence is consistent with the claimed authorship timeline and effort. Participation is opt-in: CPoE serves as a provenance tool that rewards transparency, not a surveillance mechanism that presumes guilt.

This use case requires particular attention to privacy. Behavioral telemetry constitutes biometric data; the privacy protections defined in (jitter quantization, data minimization, and Verifier data retention limits) are essential safeguards. Institutions deploying CPoE should establish clear data governance policies and ensure students retain control over their Evidence Packets.

section.name: Journalism and News Provenance
section.t: Major news organizations including the Associated Press and BBC have adopted editorial policies requiring human oversight of AI-assisted content production, and several have co-founded initiatives to combat AI-generated disinformation. These policies require reporters to disclose AI tool use but lack a machine-verifiable mechanism for enforcement.

A reporter's authoring application acts as the Attester, producing Evidence Packets during article composition. The news organization's editorial system acts as the Verifier, appraising the evidence before publication. The resulting Attestation Result can be embedded in the article's metadata for downstream consumers (fact-checkers, aggregators, and readers) who act as secondary Relying Parties. When reporters use AI tools for research or drafting, Tool Receipts document each contribution, preserving an auditable record of the human editorial effort that complements C2PA media provenance for any associated images or video.

section.name: Legal and Evidentiary Standards
section.t: CPoE Evidence Packets are designed to align with existing legal standards for digital evidence authentication. The U.S. Federal Rules of Evidence already provide a framework: Rule 901(b)(9) admits evidence about "a process or system, showing it produces an accurate result," and Rules 902(13) and 902(14) (amended 2017) establish that hash-authenticated electronic records and certified process outputs are self-authenticating. CPoE's hash-chained evidence structure, cryptographic signatures, and deterministic verification procedures map naturally to these evidentiary requirements.

Regulatory frameworks are also converging on mandatory AI content disclosure. The EU AI Act (Article 50) requires disclosure of AI-generated content published on matters of public interest, with enforcement beginning August 2026. These obligations create demand for a standardized technical mechanism that can produce verifiable, machine-readable attestation of how content was produced.

In this use case, a filer's authoring environment acts as the Attester, producing Evidence Packets bound to a hardware Secure Element (T3 or T4 tier) for non-repudiation. The regulatory body or court acts as the Relying Party, consuming Attestation Results that include forgery cost estimates to quantify the economic assurance of the evidence.

section.name: Content Platforms and Marketplaces
section.t: Content platforms may distinguish between human-authored and AI-generated submissions for editorial placement, pricing, or labeling purposes. Authors act as Attesters, submitting Evidence Packets alongside their content. The platform's Verifier produces Attestation Results that inform trust decisions.

Absence Proofs as defined in enable the platform to identify submissions that lack effort-based evidence, indicating unknown provenance rather than necessarily AI generation. The forgery cost bounds in the Attestation Result provide a quantitative basis for graduated trust: platforms can distinguish between content with strong effort-based evidence, content with partial evidence, and content with no provenance at all, rather than relying on a binary authentic-or-not classification.

section.name: Scope and Applicability
section.t: CPoE is designed as a voluntary, author-initiated mechanism. The following normative constraints define its intended scope of use and apply to all conforming implementations:

li.t: Evidence collection MUST be initiated by the author. The Attester operates under the author's control; no external party may activate evidence collection without the author's explicit consent.

Implementations MUST NOT be deployed as proctoring or surveillance mechanisms. CPoE does not capture screen content, camera input, biometric identification, or application activity outside the authoring environment.

The author MUST retain sole control over whether to share Evidence Packets with a Verifier or Relying Party. Evidence Packets are generated and stored locally until the author chooses to release them.

Verifiers MUST NOT automatically reject Evidence based solely on atypical timing patterns. Atypical input patterns may reflect assistive technologies, non-Latin input methods, or individual variation rather than forgery (see ).

section.t: Whether any institution or platform requires CPoE evidence as a condition of participation is a policy decision outside the scope of this protocol. CPoE provides a technical mechanism for producing verifiable evidence; it does not mandate that evidence be produced or consumed.

section.name: System Model
section.t: This section defines the CPoE system model in terms of the RATS architecture and identifies where CPoE diverges from standard remote attestation assumptions.

section.name: RATS Entity Roles
section.t: CPoE maps to RATS entity roles as follows. Verifier and Relying Party follow standard RATS definitions; the remaining roles have CPoE-specific characteristics:

dd.t: The authoring application and its host platform. Unlike traditional RATS deployments, the Attester is operated by the entity whose claims are being verified (the author).
The authoring application, OS entropy interfaces, and hardware Secure Elements (TPM/SE) when available.
Hardware manufacturers that issue TPM endorsement certificates and platform attestation credentials for T3/T4 tiers.
The CPoE specification itself (behavioral patterns, SWF parameters) and calibration services that provide updated forensic baselines.
The document editor session and its content state. The Target Environment is measured by the Attesting Environment at each checkpoint via content hashing and behavioral telemetry capture.

section.name: Compatibility with RATS Architecture
section.t: CPoE extends RATS from device state attestation to effort attestation, verifying that sustained human effort was expended during authorship. The fundamental problem structure is identical: an Attester generates Evidence, conveys it to a Verifier, and the Verifier produces Attestation Results for Relying Parties.

CPoE implements a critical trust inversion: in traditional remote attestation, the adversary is external (malware, network attackers). In CPoE, the Attester is operated by the author, and the primary adversary is the Attester operator themselves. This inversion shapes the security model:

li.t: Evidence must be unforgeable by the entity generating it
Temporal claims must be bound to physical constraints the Attester cannot circumvent
Behavioral entropy must be computationally expensive to simulate
Hardware attestation provides value only when the hardware root of trust is genuinely inaccessible to the Attester operator

section.t: The RATS architecture accommodates this through its layered trust model and configurable Appraisal Policies (). The companion appraisal document () defines domain-specific verification procedures. The rationale for Experimental status is provided in .

section.name: Adversarial Attester as RATS Profile
section.t: CPoE constitutes a RATS profile in which the standard Attester-operator trust assumption is explicitly relaxed. RFC 9334 Section 3 defines Attester roles functionally (the entity producing Evidence) without requiring the operator to be trusted. CPoE leverages this by treating the Attester operator as the primary adversary and relying on physics-based constraints, memory-hard functions, and hardware trust anchors (at T3/T4) rather than Attester honesty.

This profile is analogous to anti-cheat and DRM attestation patterns where the platform operator is adversarial, and differs from traditional RATS deployments (firmware integrity, supply chain verification) where external compromise is the primary threat. Implementations and Verifier policies MUST account for this trust model when interpreting CPoE Evidence.

section.name: Evidence Format and EAT Relationship
section.t: CPoE Evidence Packets use a domain-specific CBOR structure (tag 1129336645) rather than CWT/JWT-wrapped EAT tokens. This design reflects the fundamental difference between CPoE Evidence and traditional EAT claims:

li.t: EAT () models entity state as a set of claims at a point in time. CPoE Evidence models sustained effort as an ordered sequence of checkpoints with SWF proofs, behavioral entropy, and physical state bindings.
The checkpoint chain structure (sequential process-proofs, hash-linked deltas, jitter bindings) has no natural representation in the EAT claims model.
Wrapping each checkpoint as a separate EAT would lose the cryptographic chain integrity that is central to CPoE's security properties.

section.t: The EAT profile URI "urn:ietf:params:rats:eat:profile:cpoe:1.0" applies to the Attestation Result (WAR) format defined in , which carries EAT-compatible claims (verdict, attestation tier, forensic assessments). The Evidence Packet uses its own profile URI "urn:ietf:params:cpoe:profile:1.0" to identify the CPoE Evidence format. Generic EAT tooling cannot parse CPoE Evidence without CPoE-specific support, but can consume WAR Attestation Results via the EAR compatibility mapping defined in .

section.name: Reference Value Trust Model
section.t: The Reference Value Provider role in CPoE differs from traditional RATS deployments where RVPs supply known-good platform measurements from a trusted supply chain. In CPoE, Reference Values take two forms:

dd.t: SWF parameters, forensic thresholds, and profile requirements defined in this document and . These are static and trusted by virtue of the specification itself.

Per-author behavioral profiles (baseline-digest) accumulated across sessions within the Attesting Environment. These are self-asserted by the Attester and MUST NOT be treated as trusted Reference Values. The baseline-digest is signed by the Evidence Packet's signing key and bound to the author identity via identity-fingerprint, but at T1/T2 tiers the signing key is software-controlled and the baseline could be synthetically constructed (see ).

section.t: Verifiers MUST treat behavioral baselines as corroborative evidence whose weight scales with the confidence-tier (population-reference through mature), not as independent attestation of authenticity. The forensic mechanisms (SNR, CLC, error topology) operate independently of baseline data and provide the primary discrimination between biological and synthetic authoring.

section.name: Relationship to Existing Proof Systems
section.t: The "Proof of X" label invites comparison with established proof families. Most such systems prove one of a small number of things: a mathematical statement is true, a participant expended some resource, a device is in a claimed state, a record existed at a certain time, a claimant controls a secret key, or a consensus participant deserves influence. CPoE proves none of these. It proves that a piece of content emerged through a sustained, temporally extended, human-originated creation process, evidenced by a chain of cryptographically protected process observations. That makes it a different species. This section makes the boundaries explicit to prevent both overstatement and mischaracterization.

section.name: Attestation, Not Consensus
section.t: The most common misreading is to treat CPoE as a blockchain consensus mechanism. It is not. Consensus proofs (Proof of Work, Proof of Stake, Proof of Space, Proof of Elapsed Time) answer: who gets to append the next block, who gets rewarded, who has sybil resistance in a network. CPoE answers: what happened during creation, whether the process record is internally coherent, whether the evidence chain is expensive to fabricate after the fact, and whether a Verifier can distinguish process evidence from a mere end-state artifact.

The closest existing tradition is remote attestation. CPoE maps directly onto the RATS architecture , with the critical difference that traditional remote attestation asks "is this device in a trustworthy state?" while CPoE asks "did a trustworthy creation process produce this content?" The adversary model is also inverted: RATS typically measures a device to determine whether to trust it; CPoE assumes the Attester may actively fabricate the very evidence being presented. That trust inversion, detailed in , has no established precedent in the RATS ecosystem and is one of the most original aspects of this protocol.

section.name: Component Proof Families
section.t: CPoE is a composite architecture. No single existing proof family captures the full claim, but five families contribute essential components:

dl.dt: Commitment proofs (hash chains, Merkle trees, authenticated logs):

dd.t: Provide integrity, ordering, and tamper evidence. CPoE's checkpoint chain, content-hash bindings, and SWF Merkle trees are authenticated data structures in this tradition. They prove that the evidence structure has not been retroactively modified, reordered, or selectively omitted. A CPoE Evidence Packet is, at its core, a domain-specific cryptographically protected audit log for authorship-relevant process events. That framing is intentional: secure audit logs are well-understood by security engineers, and CPoE extends the paradigm from system events to creation dynamics.

dl.dt: Temporal proofs (VDFs, sequential work functions, delay constructions):

dd.t: Provide minimum elapsed time and resistance to backfilled fabrication. CPoE's SWF uses Argon2id iterations that require irreducible sequential computation, closely related to Verifiable Delay Functions. Standard VDFs prove "this output required sequential time." CPoE binds that temporal proof to document state at each checkpoint. The VDF contributes the temporal anti-compression layer; CPoE adds the content and process linkage layer on top. CPoE can be described as a higher-order evidence system that uses delay-based proofs as one subcomponent of temporal credibility.

dl.dt: Platform and process attestation (RATS, TPM-based evidence, endpoint bindings):

dd.t: Provide structured evidence claims about the capture environment with policy-based appraisal. This is the architectural skeleton of CPoE. Both systems involve Evidence, Appraisal, claims about trustworthiness, claims emitted by potentially imperfect agents, and policy-based verification. The difference is the object of attestation: platform state versus creation process.

dl.dt: Behavioral and process signals (typing cadence, revision patterns, pause structure):

dd.t: Provide discrimination between composition and transcription. Behavioral biometrics typically aim to answer "is this the same person?" CPoE borrows the same signal families but repurposes them from identity classification to process evidencing. The goal is not person recognition but process authenticity: did this content emerge through a real composition process consistent with human effort?

Provide interoperability, external embedding, and transportable claim structures. CPoE's wire format uses CBOR with COSE signatures, enabling Evidence Packets to be referenced by media provenance systems such as C2PA . Provenance systems track lineage and transformations. CPoE tracks the creation process itself. The two operate at different strata and are complementary.

section.name: Per-System Comparisons
section.t: The following comparisons address the systems most frequently confused with CPoE, organized by what each system proves and where CPoE diverges.

dd.t: PoW proves resource expenditure without semantics. CPoE proves resource expenditure bound to a semantic process trace. In PoW, the work is the point. In CPoE, the work is a binding mechanism. Both use cost imposition as a forgery deterrent, but PoW is indifferent to what the work was for. CPoE entangles every unit of work with a specific content state. CPoE inherits anti-forgery logic from PoW but uses work as evidence support, not as the object being proven.

PoET (Intel SGX) certifies that a node waited a random interval using a trusted enclave. CPoE achieves a similar temporal guarantee without requiring trusted hardware at T1/T2, and with hardware anchoring at T3/T4. PoET proves "I waited." CPoE proves "I worked continuously while content evolved." The trust model also differs sharply: PoET trusts the enclave; CPoE at lower tiers assumes a hostile endpoint and relies on forensic verification. That makes CPoE less trusting, more forensic, and a stronger fit for evidentiary settings where the claimant controls the environment.

A signed file tells you that someone with key K signed blob B. That is all. Signatures prove authorization or custody. CPoE proves generative history: that blob B came from a specific process history H, that H evolved through sequential checkpoints, and that tampering with H is detectably hard. CPoE is a layer above signatures, not a replacement for them. This distinction is load-bearing: a COSE_Sign1 wrapper on an Evidence Packet proves the signer approved it, while the Evidence Packet's internal structure proves how the content was created.

Timestamping () proves that data existed no later than time T. It does not prove how that data came to exist, whether it arose through human effort, or whether a version history was fabricated and then anchored retroactively. Timestamping gives existence provenance. CPoE gives process provenance. The SWF checkpoint chain can incorporate external timestamps (via beacon-anchor or witness services), but the timestamps are necessary support, not sufficient evidence on their own.

C2PA-style manifests track what asset came from where, what transformations occurred, and which actors signed assertions. CPoE tracks how a work was created in the first place: what evidence supports claims of human-origin effort, and how the internal composition process unfolded. Provenance systems answer "where did this come from?" CPoE answers "how was it made?" CPoE is a missing evidentiary layer that provenance systems generally lack for text, and Evidence Packets can be embedded in or referenced by C2PA manifests.

AI detectors are post-hoc classifiers that infer from the finished artifact. They are probabilistic, degrade as generative models improve, and produce no durable evidence chain. CPoE takes the opposite design philosophy: attest from the creation process rather than infer from the output. AI detection guesses from residue; CPoE preserves the chain of creation. CPoE exists in part because detector-style systems are epistemically weak (see ).

PoP systems prove that a participant is a unique human for sybil resistance. CPoE does not prove uniqueness or identity; an author may hold multiple CPoE identities without conflict. CPoE proves that human-like cognitive effort was expended during a specific authoring session. PoP makes an identity claim. CPoE makes a behavioral process claim. A CAPTCHA proves human presence at one moment; CPoE proves a human-like creation process unfolded across an extended interval. That shift from point-in-time presence to longitudinal effort evidence is a major design difference.

ZKPs prove that a statement is true without revealing the witness. CPoE is not a zero-knowledge proof in the formal cryptographic sense. It is an evidence package whose integrity can be cryptographically verified and whose semantics are judged by policy and forensic inference. Parts of the protocol could be formally verified using SNARK or STARK techniques (e.g., proving checkpoint derivation was computed correctly), and ZK techniques could enhance privacy (e.g., proving minimum session duration without revealing keystroke intervals). But the core process-authenticity claim remains empirical and evidentiary, not purely deductive. This is an important boundary: CPoE provides cryptographically supported evidentiary proof, not formal logical proof.

section.name: Structural Analogies
section.t: Two analogies outside the cryptographic proof tradition illuminate CPoE's design intent more clearly than comparisons with consensus protocols:

dd.t: Forensic chain of custody tracks who handled evidence, when, under what controls, and whether tampering occurred. CPoE is chain of custody for authorship formation. Instead of custody of a physical object after it exists, CPoE tracks custody of the evolving creation state during the act of creation itself. That shifts the evidentiary frontier from "preserve the artifact" to "preserve the process that generated the artifact."

Scientific lab notebooks establish who did what, when, experimental progression, and priority. They rely on human recordkeeping and witnesses. CPoE is the cryptographic and machine-verifiable version of the same intuition, applied to writing rather than laboratory work. The checkpoint chain is a machine-generated lab notebook whose entries are hash-linked, temporally bound, and independently auditable.

section.name: Honest Limitations
section.t: This section acknowledges the boundaries of what CPoE can and cannot prove, because reviewers will rightly probe these boundaries.

dd.t: Partly correct. Unless every claim is formally reducible to a cryptographic statement, parts of the system remain evidentiary rather than deductive. The cryptography proves chain integrity, temporal ordering, and anti-tampering properties. Policy and appraisal interpret what that evidence means. This is true of most legal-grade digital evidence systems. CPoE does not claim to be a theorem; it claims to be a well-structured, hard-to-forge evidence record.

Correct. Any human-process inference from behavior remains probabilistic. CPoE can strongly prove chain integrity and temporal properties. It can support, but not mathematically prove, human-process inferences. The strongest version of CPoE does not claim perfect detection; it claims that fabrication requires expenditure proportional to the claimed effort, and that the behavioral signals raise the cost and complexity of that fabrication.

Possibly, but at a cost. CPoE's design goal is not to make forgery impossible but to make it expensive, detectable, and time-consuming. The SWF imposes irreducible sequential computation per checkpoint. Behavioral entropy analysis detects uniform typing cadence inconsistent with composition. The forgery cost model in quantifies the economic cost of defeating each layer. The protocol is strongest when its goal is understood as raising fabrication cost and preserving early evidence, not as achieving information-theoretic impossibility of forgery.

Also partly correct, and deliberately so. Secure logging is a well-understood, battle-tested paradigm. CPoE extends it with creation-process semantics, temporal anti-compression barriers, and behavioral signals. The question is not whether CPoE is a log, but whether this particular log captures the right semantics and resists forgery well enough to be useful as authorship evidence. That is where the design work in and lives.

section.name: What is Novel
section.t: The novelty of CPoE is not in any single primitive. Hash chains, sequential work, behavioral signals, attestation architectures, and provenance packaging all exist independently. The novelty is in their composition into a single evidentiary claim: not merely that a file existed, nor that a device signed it, nor that computation was spent, but that the file emerged through a sustained, verifiable effort process that is materially harder to fabricate than ordinary drafts, logs, or post-hoc metadata.

If a reviewer asks "what existing proof system is this?" the honest answer is: none exactly. CPoE is a hybrid system drawing from secure logging, attestation, timestamping, sequential work, behavioral biometrics, and provenance packaging, assembled to prove process rather than end-state.
Proof of Work proves spent computation. Proof of Effort proves a content-linked creation history backed by cryptographic evidence.

section.name: Protocol Overview
section.t: This section provides an end-to-end overview of the CPoE protocol, mapping the message flow to the RATS passport model and illustrating the lifecycle of an Evidence Packet from creation through appraisal.

section.name: Passport Model Message Flow
section.t: CPoE follows the RATS passport model (, Section 8.1; ):

figure.artwork: +----------+ .cpoe +-----------+ .cwar +-----------+ | Attester +--------->+ Verifier +--------->+ Relying | | (Author/ |Evidence | |Attestation| Party | | AE) | | | Results |(Publisher)| +----------+ +-----+-----+ +-----------+ ^ Endorsements | Reference Values (TPM/SE certs) | (SWF params, baselines) | +------------+------------+ | Endorser / Ref. Value | | Provider | +-------------------------+

section.t: The CPoE-specific message flow is:

li.t: The Attester (authoring application running in the Attesting Environment) collects behavioral telemetry during content creation and generates an Evidence Packet (.cpoe) containing SWF proofs, jitter bindings, and physical state markers.
The Evidence Packet is conveyed to a Verifier, which appraises chain integrity, temporal ordering, behavioral entropy, and content binding per the procedures defined in .
The Verifier produces a Cryptographic Written Authorship Report (.cwar) containing EAT claims, forensic assessment scores, and forgery cost estimates.
The Relying Party (publisher, reader, or automated platform) consumes the WAR to make trust decisions about the claimed authorship provenance.

section.t: Endorsers (hardware manufacturers) supply TPM endorsement certificates and Secure Element attestations that Verifiers use to validate hardware-bound claims in T3/T4 Evidence. Reference Value Providers supply the expected behavioral patterns, SWF difficulty parameters, and profile specifications that Verifiers use as appraisal baselines.

Note: In some deployments, the Relying Party (e.g., a content management system or publishing platform) may receive an Evidence Packet alongside content and forward it to a Verifier on behalf of the author. This is operationally similar to the RATS background-check model (, Section 8.2), where the Relying Party initiates verification. However, the Evidence Packet is still generated by the Attester and travels with the content as a self-contained credential, making this architecturally consistent with the passport model. Deployments using this pattern SHOULD ensure that the Relying Party does not modify the Evidence Packet before forwarding it to the Verifier.

section.name: Evidence Lifecycle
section.t: The following sequence illustrates the end-to-end lifecycle of a CPoE attestation session:
